title: Which Way Does the Water Go?

scenes.visual: Title card 'Which Way Does the Water Go?' over a goldfish outline (left) and a cod outline (right). COLOUR MAP used in every scene of both films and in the lesson: water BLUE, sodium chloride ORANGE dots, urea GREEN, body outlines charcoal. Arrow grammar: DASHED arrow = passive leak; SOLID arrow with a small 'ATP' tag = paid transport. Every number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: A goldfish in a bowl soaks up water all day, and a cod in the sea loses it. How does each one stay the same size?
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: goldfish in a round bowl, BLUE dashed arrows pointing into its body. Right: cod in open sea, BLUE dashed arrows pointing out of its body. Each fish's outline holds steady, label 'same size, day after day' with a question mark.
scenes.narration: A goldfish in a bowl soaks up water all day, and a cod in the sea loses it. How does each one stay the same size?

scenes.tts: Start with one rule, for a surface water can cross. With nothing pushing back, water moves on its own toward the side with more dissolved particles. That count is called osmolality. In these fish, each salt leaks toward the side where it is scarcer.
scenes.visual: A membrane drawn as a vertical line. Left side has few particles, right side many. BLUE dashed arrows slide left to right across the membrane; ORANGE dots drift right to left. On-screen labels 'osmolality = dissolved particles per kilogram of water' and, small, 'assumes: water can cross, no opposing pressure; salt arrows follow charge + concentration'.
scenes.narration: Start with one rule, for a surface water can cross. With nothing pushing back, water moves on its own toward the side with more dissolved particles. That count is called osmolality. In these fish, each salt leaks toward the side where it is scarcer.

scenes.tts: Watch the bar in the corner of every tank. One mark shows the body's osmolality, and one shows the water outside. Water drifts toward the higher mark.
scenes.visual: A vertical osmolality bar appears at top right, scale 0 to 1,100 mOsm per kg. Two pointers: 'body' (charcoal) and 'outside' (BLUE). A small BLUE arrow beside the bar always points toward the higher pointer. This bar stays in the corner of every later scene.
scenes.narration: Watch the bar in the corner of every tank. One mark shows the body's osmolality, and one shows the water outside. Water drifts toward the higher mark.

scenes.tts: Now give the fish a ledger: one column for what comes in, one for what goes out. If its water and salts hold steady, the columns must match, for water and for each salt separately.
scenes.visual: A two-column ledger slides in beside a plain fish outline, headed 'In' and 'Out', with a BLUE row 'water' and an ORANGE row 'salt'. A balance-scale icon under it reads 'steady state: body water and each salt constant, so total in = total out'.
scenes.narration: Now give the fish a ledger: one column for what comes in, one for what goes out. If its water and salts hold steady, the columns must match, for water and for each salt separately.

scenes.tts: Drop a bony fish into the sea. Its blood holds far fewer dissolved particles than seawater. So water leaks out across its gills, and salt leaks in.
scenes.visual: Tank 1, labelled 'SEA'. On-screen text 'blood: about a third of seawater'. Corner bar: body pointer at '~350' (label 'illustrative'), outside at '~1,000'. BLUE dashed arrows leave the fish across the gills; ORANGE dots leak in. Ledger: BLUE 'Out' bar grows long, ORANGE 'In' bar grows; both rows flash red 'unbalanced'.
scenes.narration: Drop a bony fish into the sea. Its blood holds far fewer dissolved particles than seawater. So water leaks out across its gills, and salt leaks in.

scenes.tts: Water is short, so the fish drinks seawater. Its gut absorbs the water, but the salt comes in with it.
scenes.visual: The fish opens its mouth; a BLUE stream speckled with ORANGE dots flows into the gut. Ledger: BLUE 'In' grows to match BLUE 'Out' (water row turns green-check). ORANGE 'In' grows even longer; salt row stays red.
scenes.narration: Water is short, so the fish drinks seawater. Its gut absorbs the water, but the salt comes in with it.

scenes.tts: Now salt is the problem. Cells in the gills send sodium and chloride back out into the sea. That runs against the leak, so it costs A T P.
scenes.caption: Now salt is the problem. Cells in the gills send sodium and chloride back out into the sea. That runs against the leak, so it costs ATP.
scenes.visual: Close-up of a gill filament: SOLID ORANGE arrows with 'ATP' tags carry dots outward into the sea. Ledger: ORANGE 'Out' grows to match ORANGE 'In'; both rows show check marks. Label 'the gap sets the leak; the fish pays to return the salt'.
scenes.narration: Now salt is the problem. Cells in the gills send sodium and chloride back out into the sea. That runs against the leak, so it costs ATP.

scenes.tts: Now move a bony fish to a river. The bar flips. Its blood is far saltier than fresh water. So water pours in across the gills, and salt leaks out.
scenes.visual: Tank 2, labelled 'RIVER'. Corner bar: body pointer at '~300' (label 'illustrative'), outside near '~5'. The small BLUE arrow beside the bar flips direction. BLUE dashed arrows now enter the fish; ORANGE dots leak out. Ledger resets; BLUE 'In' and ORANGE 'Out' rows flash red.
scenes.narration: Now move a bony fish to a river. The bar flips. Its blood is far saltier than fresh water. So water pours in across the gills, and salt leaks out.

scenes.tts: The water is easy to fix. The kidney makes a large volume of dilute urine, and the extra water leaves that way.
scenes.visual: A wide BLUE stream with very few ORANGE dots flows from the fish's vent, label 'dilute urine'. Ledger: BLUE 'Out' grows to match BLUE 'In'; water row checks.
scenes.narration: The water is easy to fix. The kidney makes a large volume of dilute urine, and the extra water leaves that way.

scenes.tts: But that urine carries a little salt away, and salt keeps leaking out across the gills. What must the gills now do with salt?
scenes.visual: Two ORANGE 'Out' entries on the ledger, drawn as equal-sized placeholder boxes (schematic, sizes not compared): 'urine' and 'gill leak'. The ORANGE 'In' column is empty. Question card: 'gills: pump salt out, or pump salt in?'
scenes.narration: But that urine carries a little salt away, and salt keeps leaking out across the gills. What must the gills now do with salt?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Take it in. Gill cells pull sodium and chloride from the river water, against the leak. Again, that costs A T P.
scenes.caption: Take it in. Gill cells pull sodium and chloride from the river water, against the leak. Again, that costs ATP.
scenes.visual: SOLID ORANGE arrows with 'ATP' tags now point INTO the gill from the river. ORANGE 'In' fills to match the two 'Out' entries; salt row checks. Side-by-side thumbnails of SEA and RIVER fish: the solid ORANGE arrows point opposite ways.
scenes.narration: Take it in. Gill cells pull sodium and chloride from the river water, against the leak. Again, that costs ATP.

scenes.tts: One more tank. A shark lives in the same sea as the cod, and its blood holds less salt than seawater. Yet it does not lose water. Why not?
scenes.visual: Tank 3, labelled 'SEA', a shark outline. Corner bar: an ORANGE segment labelled 'salts' rises well short of the seawater pointer at '~1,000'. Question mark beside the shark.
scenes.narration: One more tank. A shark lives in the same sea as the cod, and its blood holds less salt than seawater. Yet it does not lose water. Why not?

scenes.tts: Its blood also carries a large load of urea, which the shark makes itself and holds on to. A little T M A O rides along. Both count as dissolved particles. With them, the blood sits just above seawater.
scenes.visual: GREEN particles flood the shark's blood vessels. On the corner bar a GREEN segment labelled 'urea' stacks on the ORANGE 'salts' segment, and a thin grey cap labelled 'TMAO' tops it, until the body pointer sits just past seawater at '~1,020' (label 'illustrative').
scenes.caption: Its blood also carries a large load of urea, which the shark makes itself and holds on to. A little TMAO rides along. Both count as dissolved particles. With them, the blood sits just above seawater.
scenes.narration: Its blood also carries a large load of urea, which the shark makes itself and holds on to. A little TMAO rides along. Both count as dissolved particles. With them, the blood sits just above seawater.

scenes.tts: So the water leak runs the other way, as a slow trickle inward. The shark need not drink seawater.
scenes.visual: The small BLUE arrow beside the bar flips to point inward. A few thin BLUE dashed arrows enter the shark's gills slowly. The drinking icon from the SEA tank appears over the shark and is crossed out.
scenes.narration: So the water leak runs the other way, as a slow trickle inward. The shark need not drink seawater.

scenes.tts: Three tanks, one budget. The gap between body and water sets which way the leaks run. Drinking, urine and paid salt transport close each gap.
scenes.visual: The three tanks shrink side by side, each with its corner bar and ledger. DASHED arrows (leaks) in each tank pulse first, then the routes that answer them: a drinking icon (sea fish), a urine stream (river fish), SOLID ATP-tagged salt arrows (both fish). The two bony-fish ledgers show green checks, 'balanced'. The shark's ledger shows its slow water inflow and salt leak with an open 'Out' column, stamped 'incomplete here: output routes in the lesson'. Label across the bottom: 'total gains = total losses'.
scenes.narration: Three tanks, one budget. The gap between body and water sets which way the leaks run. Drinking, urine and paid salt transport close each gap.

scenes.visual: End card with the Hex mascot holding a balanced two-column ledger. Take-home line: 'Gains must equal losses, for water and each salt.'
